vignette:
The Weight of What He Witnessed

Boon-Nam is a 72-year-old Thai man who has spent the better part of four decades helping others survive the worst moments of their lives. He has resettled families, translated across languages and cultures, and sat with people whose losses were beyond articulation. He thought he understood trauma — understood it the way a man understands the ocean from the shore. Then a morning came that pulled him under.

Three years ago, Boon-Nam was accompanying a group of newly arrived refugees through a processing center in a border region when a coordinated attack struck the compound. The explosion came without warning. He remembers the sound before he remembers anything else — not a bang, he says, but a pressure, something that pushed the world sideways. When he came to, he was on the ground, his ears ringing, and there was a young woman nearby who had been helping him with translation. She was not moving. He crawled toward her. He has never spoken about what he found, only that he could not help her, and that he stayed beside her until someone pulled him away.

Boon-Nam was physically unharmed. He returned home to his wife, Malee, in Bangkok within two weeks. He told her he was fine. He told his organization he was fine. He filed his incident report and requested reassignment to administrative duties, framing it as a preference for slowing down at his age. For nearly a year, he believed his own explanation.

But sleep became its own ordeal. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, his heart hammering, the smell of smoke so vivid he has gotten up to check the kitchen. The dreams are not always dramatic — sometimes he simply dreams that he is back on the floor of the compound, and the young woman is looking at him, waiting for him to do something. He wakes before he can.

During the day, Boon-Nam moves through the world with a vigilance that exhausts him. He avoids crowded public spaces, which is no small thing in Bangkok. He no longer takes the skytrain during peak hours. When a truck backfires on the street below his office, he drops instinctively, and then spends the next hour managing the shame of having done so. He does not tell Malee about these moments. He has always been the steady one in their marriage, the one who absorbed difficulty quietly, and he does not know how to stop performing that role even now.

His work has narrowed considerably. He continues to consult for his organization but declines field assignments with explanations that are technically true — his knees, his age, the logistics. He reads case files about people fleeing violence and finds himself unable to finish them, setting them aside and returning to administrative tasks that require nothing of his imagination. He recognizes something is being lost in him, some capacity that once felt like his greatest professional gift — the ability to sit fully present with another person's suffering — and the recognition of that loss sits heavily on him.

He is not a man who speaks easily about inner states. He was raised to carry difficulty with dignity, and he has done so for seven decades with considerable success. What brings him to therapy is not his own distress, exactly, but his wife's quiet alarm. Malee told him one evening, without accusation, that she felt she was living with someone who had come back from the border and left part of himself there. He did not argue with her. He knew she was right.

He sits in the therapy room with his hands folded in his lap, composed and courteous, choosing his words with care. But occasionally, when the conversation moves close to that morning, something shifts in his eyes — a flatness, a going-away — and for a moment the 72-year-old man with the careful posture is back on a concrete floor, unable to help, staying anyway.
